item.title: Beyond straight lines
item.description:
Beyond straight lines#

Every model so far was linear in its inputs, plus whatever products and powers we chose to add by hand (in Lecture 2 we had to decide to add \(G \times T\) or to take \(\ln V\)). This page introduces models that find the shape of a curve from the data: step functions, regression splines, smoothing splines, local regression and generalised additive models. The running example is the electricity demand of an office building through the day.

item.title: Logistic regression
item.description:
Logistic regression#

In Lectures 1 and 2 the output was mostly a number. Now the output is a category: a machine is healthy or faulty, a milk sample pure or adulterated, a sensor reading normal or an anomaly. This page develops the most widely used classifier, logistic regression: the model, how to read its coefficients, how it is fitted by maximum likelihood, and how its probabilities become decisions.

Notation on this page

item.title: Neural networks
item.description:
Neural networks#

With SVMs, splines and trees, a person chooses the inputs. Neural networks can start from raw measurements (pixels, samples of a signal) and build useful features themselves in their hidden layers. A network is assembled from pieces met in earlier lectures: linear models, the sigmoid, loss and cost, gradient descent and the ridge penalty. This page puts them together, explains how a network is trained (backpropagation), and shows how to stop it overfitting.

item.title: Principal components analysis
item.description:
Principal components analysis#

In Lectures 2–7 every example had an output \(Y\) to predict: that is supervised learning. In unsupervised learning there are only inputs \(X_1, \dots, X_p\), and no right answer to check against. That makes results harder to judge (there is no test error), so they must be checked against knowledge of the problem. There are two main goals:

  • summarise many variables with a few: principal components analysis (this page);
  • find groups of similar objects: clustering.

Notation on this page

item.title: Resampling
item.description:
Resampling#

The rule of Lecture 1 is to choose a model by its test error. With simulated data we could generate thousands of new test points. A real project usually has one data set, often small. This page shows how to estimate the test error from that one data set by cross-validation, and how to find the uncertainty of almost any estimate by the bootstrap. Both work by resampling: reusing the data we have in different ways.

item.title: Simple linear regression
item.description:
Simple linear regression#

Linear regression is the simplest supervised method for predicting a number, and the foundation for much of what follows. This page fits a straight line to data by least squares, using the calibration of a temperature sensor as the running example, and then asks how far the result can be trusted: standard errors, \(t\)-statistics, \(p\)-values, and \(R^2\).

In the language of Lecture 1, linear regression is the simplest example of each ingredient:

item.title: The maximal margin classifier
item.description:
The maximal margin classifier#

Trees cut the input space into boxes. Support vector machines take a different view of classification: look for the widest possible gap between the classes, and, if needed, bend that gap into a curve. This page covers the first step, for classes that a straight line can separate completely: hyperplanes, the margin, and support vectors.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
g/mL, mS/cm grams per millilitre (density); millisiemens per centimetre (electrical conductivity)
\(X_1\), \(X_2\) the two inputs (standardised density and conductivity of a milk sample)
\(p\) number of inputs
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \beta_2\) coefficients that set the position and tilt of the separating line
\(f(x)\) \(\beta_0 + \beta_1x_1 + \beta_2x_2\): its sign gives the class
\(y_i\) class of point \(i\), coded \(+1\) or \(-1\)
\(M\) the margin: distance from the line to the nearest point (half the width of the “street”)
\(w\), \(b\) scikit-learn's names for the coefficients \((\beta_1, \beta_2)\) and the intercept \(\beta_0\)
\(\lVert w\rVert\) “length of w” \(\sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2}\)

item.title: What is machine learning?
item.description:
What is machine learning?#

This page answers three questions: what machine learning is, why we need it, and how every machine-learning method can be described by the same three ingredients. It ends with the vocabulary used throughout the course and the main types of machine learning.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
\(T\) the task a program must perform
\(P\) the performance measure: the number that scores how well the task is done
\(E\) the experience: the data the program learns from

A definition#

Artificial intelligence (AI) is the broad goal of making computers perform tasks that seem to require intelligence. Machine learning (ML) is the part of AI in which the computer learns how to do a task from examples, instead of following rules written for it by a person. In short, machine learning lets computers learn from data without being explicitly programmed.

item.title: Clustering
item.description:
Clustering#

Clustering looks for groups of similar objects in data that carry no labels. This page covers the two standard methods, \(k\)-means and hierarchical clustering, using the daily electricity profiles of a utility's customers, and shows why the choice of scaling decides what the clusters will be.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
profile a customer's energy use in each of the 24 hours of a typical day (24 numbers)
\(k\) number of clusters, chosen by us
centre the average of all the profiles in a cluster
distance between two profiles \(x\) and \(x'\): \(\sqrt{\sum_j (x_j - x'_j)^2}\), summed over the 24 hours (as in KNN)
within-cluster variation total squared distance from each customer to its cluster centre
linkage how the distance between two clusters is defined in hierarchical clustering
dendrogram the tree diagram that records every merge in hierarchical clustering
adjusted Rand index agreement between two groupings: 1 = identical, 0 = no better than chance

Example: electricity customers#

A utility has smart-meter data for 300 customers: the energy each one uses in each hour of a typical day, 24 numbers per customer. Are there groups of customers with similar daily patterns? Time-of-use tariffs and the planning of transformers both depend on when customers draw power.

item.title: Convolutional networks
item.description:
Convolutional networks#

Images are where neural networks shine. A convolutional neural network (CNN) looks for the same small pattern everywhere in an image, using a few shared weights. This page shows why an ordinary network struggles with images, how convolution and pooling work, and how a small CNN detects faulty circuit boards from thermal images.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
pixel one square of an image; here each holds a temperature (\(^\circ\)C)
\(24 \times 24\) image size: 24 rows by 24 columns of pixels
filter a small grid of weights (e.g. \(3 \times 3\)) slid across the image
feature map the image of filter responses: large where the image looks like the filter
channel one feature map (or the single temperature map of the input image)
\(8 \times 12 \times 12\) 8 feature maps, each 12 by 12 pixels
\(a\), \(b\) numbers of input and output channels of a convolution layer
max pooling replace each \(2 \times 2\) block by its largest value
global max each feature map reports only its strongest response, anywhere in the image
AUC area under the ROC curve (Lecture 3)

Example: thermal images of circuit boards#

Infrared (thermal) cameras are used to inspect electronics: a failing component or a bad solder joint runs hot. A thermal camera photographs each board in operation, giving a \(24 \times 24\) image whose pixels are temperatures in \(^\circ\)C.

item.title: How good is a classifier?
item.description:
How good is a classifier?#

The error rate of Lecture 1 counts mistakes, but it does not say which mistakes a classifier makes, and in practice the two kinds of mistake can have very different costs. This page introduces the confusion matrix, the measures built from it, the choice of threshold, and the ROC curve. The example is the two-sensor machine classifier of the previous page, judged on its 2000 test machines.

item.title: Multiple linear regression
item.description:
Multiple linear regression#

Most outputs depend on more than one input. This page extends linear regression to many inputs, writes it in matrix form, solves it with the normal equations, and shows how categories, interactions and curved laws all fit into the same framework. The running example is a solar panel whose power depends on both sunlight and temperature.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(p\) number of inputs (not a \(p\)-value)
\(X_j\), \(\beta_j\) input number \(j\) and its coefficient, \(j = 1, \dots, p\)
\(x_{ij}\) value of input \(j\) in observation \(i\) (row \(i\), column \(j\))
\(\mathbf X\) “bold X” data matrix, \(n \times (p+1)\), with a first column of ones
\(\mathbf y\) “bold y” column of the \(n\) outputs
\(\boldsymbol\beta\) “bold beta” column of the coefficients \(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\)
\(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\) “bold epsilon” column of the \(n\) random errors
\(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\) “beta hat” least-squares estimates of all coefficients
\(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\) “X transpose” \(\mathbf X\) with rows and columns swapped
\(A^{-1}\) “A inverse” the matrix that undoes \(A\): \(A^{-1}A = I\)
\(I\) identity matrix: 1s on the diagonal, 0s elsewhere
\(G\) irradiance: solar power per unit area (W/m\(^2\)); full sun is about 1000 W/m\(^2\)
\(T\) cell temperature (\(^\circ\)C)
\(P\) electrical output power of the panel (W)
\(r\) correlation coefficient between two inputs, from \(-1\) to \(1\)
\(D\) dummy variable: 1 for one category (e.g. dusty), 0 for the other (clean)
\(k\) number of categories (levels) of a qualitative input
\(X_1X_2\) interaction: the product of two inputs, used as a new input
\(a\), \(\gamma\) “a”, “gamma” panel constant (W per W/m\(^2\)); loss of efficiency per \(^\circ\)C
\(V_0\), \(\tau\) “V nought”, “tau” capacitor voltage at \(t = 0\) (V); time constant \(RC\) (s)
\(\ln\) natural logarithm: \(\ln e^a = a\)

item.title: Notation and matrix algebra
item.description:
Notation and matrix algebra#

Machine learning works with tables of numbers, and tables of numbers are matrices. This page fixes the notation used in the whole course (it is the notation of the textbook ISLP) and reviews the only two matrix operations we need: the transpose and the matrix product.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(n\) number of observations (rows of the data table)
\(p\) number of inputs (columns of the data table)
\(i\), \(j\) indices: \(i = 1,\dots,n\) counts observations, \(j = 1,\dots,p\) counts inputs
\(x_{ij}\) “x i j” input \(j\) of observation \(i\): first subscript = row, second = column
\(\mathbf X\) “bold X” the whole table of inputs, \(n\) rows by \(p\) columns (bold capitals are matrices)
\(x_i\) row \(i\) of \(\mathbf X\): the \(p\) inputs of observation \(i\)
\(y_i\) the output (label) of observation \(i\)
\(\mathbf X^{\mathsf T}\) “X transpose” \(\mathbf X\) with rows and columns swapped
\(r \times d\) “r by d” the size of a matrix with \(r\) rows and \(d\) columns
\(a_{ik}\) the number in row \(i\), column \(k\) of a matrix \(A\)
\(\sum_{k=1}^{d}\) “sum from k = 1 to d” add the terms for \(k = 1, 2, \dots, d\) (capital Greek sigma)
\(\boldsymbol\beta\) “bold beta” a column of \(p\) parameters, one per input
\(\hat y_i\) “y hat i” the model's prediction for observation \(i\); a hat always means “estimated”
\(\hat{\mathbf y}\) “bold y hat” the column of all \(n\) predictions

Data as a table#

A data set is a table. Each row is one observation, each column one measured quantity. As an example, here are readings from a solar panel: the sunlight power falling on each square metre of panel (the irradiance, in W/m\(^2\)), the temperature of the solar cells, and the electrical power produced.

item.title: Regularisation
item.description:
Regularisation#

When a model has almost as many inputs as there are observations, least squares fits the noise. This page shows two ways out: choosing a subset of the inputs, and regularisation, which keeps all the inputs but shrinks their coefficients towards zero. The two regularised methods, ridge regression and the lasso, are tuned by the cross-validation of the previous page.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(n\), \(p\) number of observations (50 milk samples), number of inputs (40 sensor channels)
channel one gas sensor in the array: one input
RSS residual sum of squares \(\sum_i (y_i - \hat y_i)^2\)
\(\lambda\) “lambda” penalty strength, \(\lambda \ge 0\): a hyperparameter we choose (scikit-learn calls it alpha, which is not the step size \(\alpha\) of gradient descent)
\(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\beta_j^2\) sum of the squared coefficients of the \(p\) inputs (the intercept \(\beta_0\) is not included)
\(\lvert\beta_j\rvert\) “absolute value of beta j” the size of \(\beta_j\) without its sign, e.g. \(\lvert -0.7\rvert = 0.7\)
\(s\) a “budget” on the size of the coefficients, equivalent to \(\lambda\)
\(2^{40}\) the number of ways to choose a subset of 40 inputs (each input is either in or out)

Too many inputs: an electronic nose#

An electronic nose is an array of gas sensors. Each channel is a metal-oxide or polymer sensor that responds to a range of volatile compounds, each a little differently, so a sample gives a pattern of readings. An adulterant (a substance added illegally to milk, such as water or urea) changes that pattern.

item.title: The support vector classifier
item.description:
The support vector classifier#

Real data overlap: usually no straight line separates the classes perfectly, and then the maximal margin classifier of the previous page has no solution. The support vector classifier allows some points inside the street, or even on the wrong side, at a price set by a cost parameter \(C\).

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
violation a point inside the street or on the wrong side of the line
\(\varepsilon_i\) “epsilon i” slack of point \(i\): how far it violates the margin
\(C\) cost parameter; in scikit-learn the price per unit of slack (see the warning below about ISLP's opposite convention)
\(w\), \(\lVert w\rVert\) coefficients of the line, and their length \(\sqrt{w_1^2 + w_2^2}\)

A soft margin#

The support vector classifier, also called the soft margin classifier, allows some points inside the street or on the wrong side of the line, but makes us pay for each such violation. Each point gets a slack variable \(\varepsilon_i\) (ISLP Section 9.2.2):

item.title: Tree-based methods
item.description:
Tree-based methods#

A decision tree predicts by asking a short series of yes/no questions about the inputs. Trees are easy to explain and find interactions and thresholds by themselves, but a single tree is unstable. This page grows and prunes a tree, then combines many trees into the most accurate methods so far: bagging, random forests and boosting.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
node, leaf a question in the tree; an end of the tree, which gives the prediction
depth the largest number of questions on a path from the top of the tree to a leaf
pure a group in which all machines belong to one class
\(\hat p_k\) fraction of the machines in a group that belong to class \(k\)
\(G\) Gini index of a group: \(G = \sum_k \hat p_k(1 - \hat p_k)\), a measure of impurity
greedy picks the best split now, not the best tree overall
\(\alpha\) pruning penalty per leaf (not the step size of gradient descent)
\(B\) number of trees (bootstrap samples) in bagging, random forests or boosting
\(p\) number of inputs (6 here)
\(m\) number of inputs offered at random at each split of a random forest
\(\sigma^2\), \(\rho\) variance of one tree's prediction; correlation between two trees' predictions
\(\lambda\) learning rate (shrinkage) of boosting: each tree's weight (not the ridge penalty)
\(d\) depth of each boosting tree (not a polynomial degree); \(d = 1\) is a single question, a “stump”
OOB out-of-bag: rows not in a tree's bootstrap sample

item.title: Course wrap-up
item.description:
Course wrap-up#

A look back over the whole course, and a guide to choosing a method for a problem of your own.

The course at a glance#

Lecture Main idea Example used
1 Introduction training versus test error; bias–variance cooling cup, KNN on motors
2 Linear regression least squares; SE and \(t\); gradient descent sensor calibration, solar panel
3 Classification logistic regression; ROC; LDA, QDA motor faults
4 Resampling, regularisation cross-validation; bootstrap; lasso thermistor, electronic nose
5 Non-linear models, trees splines; random forests; boosting building demand, six-sensor machines
6 Support vector machines maximal margin; kernels milk adulteration, shaft orbit
7 Neural networks backpropagation; CNNs; RNNs thermal images, demand forecasting

The thread through all eight lectures: fit on training data, judge on new data.

item.title: Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes
item.description:
Generative models: LDA, QDA, naive Bayes#

Logistic regression models the probability of each class directly. This page takes another route: describe what each class looks like, then use Bayes' theorem to work out which class a new observation most probably belongs to. It covers linear and quadratic discriminant analysis and naive Bayes, compares all the classifiers met so far on the same test data, and extends classification to more than two classes.

item.title: Gradient descent
item.description:
Gradient descent#

For linear regression the normal equations give the best coefficients directly. Most later models (logistic regression, neural networks) have no such formula; they are trained by gradient descent, which walks downhill on the error step by step. We learn it here, on linear regression, because the right answer is already known, so we can watch the method find it.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(\ell_i\) “ell i” loss of data point \(i\): how wrong the model is on that one point
\(J(\boldsymbol\beta)\) “J of beta” cost: the average loss over all \(n\) points; it depends on the coefficients \(\boldsymbol\beta\)
\(\alpha\) “alpha” step size, also called the learning rate; chosen by us
\(\dfrac{dJ}{d\beta}\) “d J d beta” ordinary derivative: slope of \(J\) when there is one coefficient
\(\dfrac{\partial J}{\partial\beta_j}\) “partial J partial beta j” partial derivative: slope of \(J\) when only \(\beta_j\) changes
\(\nabla J\) “grad J” gradient: the list of all partial derivatives \((\partial J/\partial\beta_0, \dots, \partial J/\partial\beta_p)\)
\(\leftarrow\) “becomes” assignment: the new value on the right replaces the old one
\(\mathbf y - \mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta\) the column of all \(n\) residuals
\(x_i\) row \(i\) of \(\mathbf X\): the inputs of data point \(i\), with the 1 for the intercept
\(z\) a standardised input (no units)
\(s\) standard deviation of an input: the typical distance of its values from their average

Loss and cost#

Two words appear in every later lecture and in every software library, often used loosely.

item.title: Kernels
item.description:
Kernels#

Some boundaries are not straight. This page shows how a support vector classifier can draw curved boundaries by working, implicitly, with extra inputs: the kernel trick. A support vector classifier with a kernel is called a support vector machine (SVM).

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(x\), \(y\) the two probe readings: shaft position in two perpendicular directions (\(\mu\)m)
\(\mu\)m “micrometre” a thousandth of a millimetre
\(r\) distance of the shaft from the centre, \(\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\) (\(\mu\)m)
feature space the set of all inputs (features) the model uses
\(x_i\), \(x_{ij}\) training point \(i\); input \(j\) of point \(i\)
\(\sum_j\) add over the inputs \(j\)
\(K(x_i, x_k)\) “kernel of x i and x k” a similarity between points \(i\) and \(k\) (not the \(K\) of KNN)
\(d\) degree of the polynomial kernel
\(\gamma\) “gamma” width parameter of the radial kernel: how fast the similarity falls with distance
\(\exp(a)\) \(e^a\)
\(C\) cost parameter (scikit-learn convention: small \(C\) = wide street)

Example: a shaft orbit#

Large turbines, compressors and pumps carry two proximity probes at right angles. These eddy-current sensors measure the gap to the rotating shaft without touching it, giving the shaft's position \(x\), \(y\) in \(\mu\)m. Plotting \(y\) against \(x\) traces the shaft's orbit.

item.title: Recurrent networks
item.description:
Recurrent networks#

A convolutional network shares weights across space. A recurrent neural network (RNN) shares them across time: it reads a sequence one step at a time and carries a memory forward. This page explains the idea and uses it to forecast a building's electricity demand.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
\(t\) time step (here, hour)
\(x_t\) input at time step \(t\) (e.g. the demand in hour \(t\))
\(h_t\) hidden state at time \(t\): the network's memory
\(W\), \(U\), \(b\) weights applied to the previous hidden state, weights applied to the new input, and a bias
\(g\) activation function
GRU, LSTM gated recurrent unit; long short-term memory: recurrent units with “gates” that remember over longer spans
AR(1), AR(24) autoregressive models: the next value is a linear function of the last 1 (or 24) values plus noise
kW\(^2\) unit of the test MSE (squared error of a demand in kW)

Sequences and memory#

A recurrent network reads a sequence \(x_1, x_2, \dots\) one step at a time. Its hidden state \(h_t\) carries a memory of what came before, and is updated at every step:

item.title: Statistical learning
item.description:
Statistical learning#

This page sets up the mathematical picture behind every method in the course: an output that depends on some inputs through an unknown function, plus random noise. Learning means estimating that function from data. We first recall two words from statistics, the expected value and the variance, because the rest of the course uses them constantly.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(Z\); \(z_1, z_2, \dots\) a random quantity (it changes each time we measure it); its measured values
\(\mathbb E(Z)\) “expected value of Z” the average of \(Z\) over very many repeats
\(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\) “variance of Z” the average squared distance of \(Z\) from its average
\(\sigma\) “sigma” standard deviation \(= \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}}\): the typical size of the spread
\(X = (X_1, \dots, X_p)\) the inputs in general; \(X_j\) is the \(j\)-th input
\(Y\) the output in general
\(f\) the true relation between inputs and output: fixed, but unknown
\(\varepsilon\) “epsilon” random error (noise): average zero, unrelated to \(X\)
\(\hat f\), \(\hat Y\) “f hat”, “Y hat” our estimate of \(f\), and its prediction \(\hat Y = \hat f(X)\)
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\) “beta nought, beta one, …” parameters of a model

Expected value and variance#

A random quantity \(Z\) takes a different value each time it is measured, like the reading of a noisy thermometer. We write its measured values as \(z_1, z_2, \dots\).

item.title: Assessing model accuracy
item.description:
Assessing model accuracy#

How do we tell a good model from a bad one? This page introduces the standard score for regression, the mean squared error, and uses a cooling cup of tea to show the most important lesson in machine learning: a model must be judged on data it has not seen. That lesson leads to the bias–variance trade-off.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
\(y_i\) measured output of observation \(i\)
\(\hat f(x_i)\) the model's prediction for observation \(i\) (also written \(\hat y_i\))
\(y_i - \hat f(x_i)\) the error (residual) of observation \(i\): measured minus predicted
\(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\) add over all \(n\) observations and divide by \(n\): the average
MSE mean squared error; units of \(y\) squared (e.g. \(^\circ\)C\(^2\))
RMSE root mean squared error \(= \sqrt{\mathrm{MSE}}\); units of \(y\)
\(\hat T\), \(t\) predicted temperature (\(^\circ\)C) and time (min) in the cooling example
\(a_0, \dots, a_d\) the coefficients (parameters) of a polynomial
\(d\) degree of a polynomial: its highest power
\(x_0\), \(y_0\) a new input (not in the training data) and its measured output
\(\operatorname{Var}(\hat f(x_0))\) variance of the model: how much its prediction at \(x_0\) changes from one training set to another
\(\operatorname{Bias}(\hat f(x_0))\) bias of the model: its average prediction at \(x_0\) minus the true \(f(x_0)\)
\(\operatorname{Var}(\varepsilon) = \sigma^2\) variance of the noise: the irreducible error

item.title: SVMs in practice
item.description:
SVMs in practice#

This page covers SVMs with more than two classes, explains why SVMs and logistic regression so often give similar answers, and lists the practical points to watch.

Notation on this page

Symbol Meaning
\(K\) number of classes
\(f(x_i)\) the SVM's (or logistic regression's) linear score for point \(i\); its sign gives the class
\(y_i\) class of point \(i\), coded \(+1\) or \(-1\)
\(y_i f(x_i)\) signed distance: positive on the correct side, negative on the wrong side, large when far on the correct side
hinge loss the SVM's loss, \(\max(0,\ 1 - y_i f(x_i))\): zero outside the street, rising in a straight line inside it
log loss the loss of logistic regression (the cross-entropy of Lecture 3)

item.title: Classification
item.description:
Classification#

When the output is a category, the mean squared error no longer makes sense. This page introduces the error rate, the ideal (but unreachable) Bayes classifier, and a first practical method, \(K\)-nearest neighbours.

Notation on this page

Symbol Read as Meaning
\(y_i\), \(\hat y_i\) true and predicted class of observation \(i\)
\(\neq\) “is not equal to”
\(I(\cdot)\) “indicator of …” 1 if the statement in brackets is true, 0 if false
\(j\) a class, e.g. healthy or faulty
\(\Pr(\cdot)\) “probability of …” a number between 0 and 1
\(\mid\) “given” \(\Pr(Y = j \mid X = x_0)\): the probability that the class is \(j\), given that the input is \(x_0\)
\(K\) the number of neighbours that vote in KNN
\(\mathcal N_0\) “N nought” the set of the \(K\) training points nearest to \(x_0\)
\(i \in \mathcal N_0\) “i in N nought” observation \(i\) is one of those neighbours

The error rate#
